title: Subfolder deny lists compare path segments case-sensitively, so a paired device can read and write host-denied folders on case-insensitive filesystems
impact: The host-configured per-subfolder read and write restrictions are fully bypassed: the device can read, zip-download, upload into, rename, move and trash files in folders the host explicitly denied. Access stays inside the device's own subtree.
description: The client-supplied path (`/files/<path>`, upload `path=`, file-ops `path=`/`to=`, zip `path=`) is lexically normalized, and its first segment is checked with an exact, case-sensitive `TreeSet.contains` against deny-list entries copied from disk with their exact case (ServerWindow.showSubfoldersDialog). The same path is then handed to java.nio Files APIs, which resolve it under the filesystem's own rules. The project targets Windows and macOS (README.md:12), whose default filesystems (NTFS, APFS) are case-insensitive, so `PRIVATE` passes the check and still opens `Private`. This follows from the code plus documented platform behaviour; I did not run it. Windows' trailing-dot stripping (`Private.`), 8.3 short names (`PRIVAT~1`) and macOS NFC/NFD Unicode equivalence are the same class of weakness, but I am less sure of those variants.
exploit_scenario: The host blocks device 'kid' from reading or writing the subfolder 'Private' in its tree. From the kid device the attacker requests GET /files/PRIVATE/taxes.pdf. firstSegment returns 'PRIVATE', which is not in denyRead={'Private'}, so the check passes, and NTFS/APFS opens Private/taxes.pdf and streams it. GET /api/zip?path=PRIVATE downloads the whole folder the same way. POST /api/upload/init?path=PRIVATE/x.txt (topFolder 'PRIVATE') followed by chunk/complete writes a file into the write-denied folder. POST /api/files/delete?path=PRIVATE/taxes.pdf or move?path=PRIVATE/...&to=public moves files out of it.
preconditions: Host runs localReceiver on a case-insensitive filesystem (Windows NTFS or macOS APFS/HFS+ default)
Pairing mode, with the host having unticked Read or Write for a subfolder in the device's subfolder dialog (deny list configured)
Attacker holds a paired device session (or a stolen session cookie) for that device
recommendation: Do not authorize by comparing raw strings. Resolve the target, and each deny-listed folder under the device root, to a canonical form (for example toRealPath() on the deepest existing ancestor, or Files.isSameFile against the denied folder) and compare those. At minimum, compare case-insensitively and NFC-normalized on case-insensitive platforms, and reject segments with trailing dots or spaces, or containing '~', before the deny-list check. Apply the same fix in canWriteSub (line 75) and UploadHandler.topFolder.

title: GET /files/ does not exclude the internal staging and trash directories, exposing other devices' in-flight uploads and trashed files
impact: Confidentiality: other devices' deleted files and partially uploaded files can be read, and the per-subfolder read deny list is bypassed for content that passes through staging or the trash. Device ids and transfer keys are also disclosed.
description: The client path in /files/<path> is only checked to stay under the device root. FileOpsHandler.resolveSafe (lines 157-159) and ZipHandler (lines 58-59) also reject targets under fileRoot/.localreceiver-part and fileRoot/.localreceiver-trash, but FilesHandler does not; the PART_DIR/TRASH filter at lines 146-147 only hides those names from listings. A device whose root is the whole file root can therefore list and download the shared staging and recycle-bin areas directly, even though TrashHandler documents that trash items are visible only to the deleting device.
exploit_scenario: A device scoped to the whole root, with 'Private' deny-listed for reading, sends GET /files/.localreceiver-trash/ to list every trash item id from all devices, then GET /files/.localreceiver-trash/<id>/meta.properties and /files/.localreceiver-trash/<id>/item/<name> to download files another device deleted from 'Private' or from its own folder. GET /files/.localreceiver-part/ enumerates every device id and upload key (`<deviceId>-<key>`), and /files/.localreceiver-part/<id>-<key>/N.chunk returns the raw chunks of other devices' in-progress uploads, including uploads bound for folders this device may not read.
preconditions: Pairing mode with a device whose folder the host has set to the whole shared root (relPath ""), which is not the default
For the deny-list bypass, the host has deny-listed some subfolders for that device
category: Files or Directories Accessible to External Parties
recommendation: In FilesHandler.handle, reject (403/404) any target that starts with fileRoot.resolve(UploadHandler.PART_DIR) or fileRoot.resolve(TrashHandler.DIR), matching FileOpsHandler.resolveSafe. Better, put one shared resolve-and-confine helper in front of every handler. Also make FileOpsHandler.rename reject the reserved names (use the same check sanitizePath applies), so a device cannot create these directories by renaming.

title: A read-denied subfolder can be renamed or moved to a new name, which escapes the name-keyed read deny list
impact: Full read access to a folder the host explicitly marked unreadable for that device, plus the deny protection is removed for every other device restricted by the same folder name.
description: File operations from a paired device are authorized only with canWriteSub on the source/destination's first segment. The read deny list is keyed by folder name, so a device that may write to a read-denied top-level folder can rename it (line 186) or move it (line 145). The data then sits under a name the deny list does not cover, and /files/ and /api/zip serve it.
exploit_scenario: The host hides the folder `private` from device A (relPath "") by unticking only its Read box, which is the natural way to hide a folder. Write stays allowed by default. A sends `POST /api/files/rename?path=private&to=loot`. resolveSafe accepts it, canWriteSub("private") is true and the folder is renamed. A then sends `GET /api/zip?path=loot` (canReadSub("loot") is true) and downloads everything. `POST /api/files/move?path=private&to=<some readable folder>` gives the same result. The rename also strips the deny entry from every other device that had `private` denied.
preconditions: Attacker holds a paired device token with the device-level Write grant
The host denied Read but not Write on a top-level subfolder (the GUI allows this; write is allowed by default)
recommendation: Treat moving, renaming or deleting an entry as requiring read access too: check canReadSub on the source in rename/move/delete. Refuse to rename or move any top-level folder that appears in denyRead or denyWrite. Alternatively, make denyRead imply denyWrite, or bind deny entries to something the device cannot rename (e.g. a stable folder identity kept server-side).

title: /files/ serves the shared trash and upload staging folders, exposing other devices' deleted files and in-flight uploads and bypassing deny lists
impact: Confidentiality breach of other devices' deleted files and partial uploads, including content from folders the host denied to the reader. This breaks the documented per-device recycle-bin isolation.
description: The client-supplied /files/ path is checked only for confinement to the device root and for the first-segment deny list. Unlike FileOpsHandler and ZipHandler, it does not exclude `.localreceiver-trash` or `.localreceiver-part`. All devices' deleted items and upload chunks are stored under the file root, so a device scoped to the whole root can list and download them directly. The TrashHandler ownership check (device id in meta.properties) and the deny lists never run on this path.
exploit_scenario: Device A has been widened to the whole shared folder (relPath "") but has denyRead {"bob"}. Device B is scoped to `bob`. B deletes bob/tax.pdf, which moves it to <root>/.localreceiver-trash/1759650000000-3fa2/item/tax.pdf. A sends `GET /files/.localreceiver-trash/` with Accept: application/json and gets every trash item id. It reads `/files/.localreceiver-trash/<id>/meta.properties` (origPath, deleting device id) and downloads `/files/.localreceiver-trash/<id>/item/tax.pdf`. In the same way, `GET /files/.localreceiver-part/` and `/files/.localreceiver-part/<Bid>-<key>/<n>.chunk` expose B's in-progress or abandoned uploads into the denied folder.
preconditions: Attacker holds a paired device token whose folder is the whole shared root (relPath ""), granted by the host
Another device has deleted files or has staged uploads, typically from a folder the attacker is denied
recommendation: In FilesHandler.handle, reject (403/404) any target that starts with fileRoot.resolve(UploadHandler.PART_DIR) or fileRoot.resolve(TrashHandler.DIR), matching resolveSafe in FileOpsHandler. Better, move staging and trash outside the served file root.

title: CA fingerprint shown to the user is a separate server response, not the fingerprint of the certificate the device installs, so the out-of-band check does not stop CA substitution
impact: The attacker's root CA is installed permanently in the victim device's trust store. The attacker can then issue trusted certificates for any hostname and intercept or modify all of that device's HTTPS traffic (banking, email, localReceiver session cookies) wherever they hold an on-path position. Even the real localReceiver CA is unconstrained (TlsSupport.generateCa adds no name-constraints extension), so the 'can only vouch for that computer's own localReceiver servers' claim in cert-help.html:26-27 does not hold either. This is an incomplete fix for the 'CA substitution during first pairing' issue that commit 19d0aec set out to address.
description: cert-check.js gets the 'Certificate SHA-256' it shows from its own GET /ca-fingerprint request, over the same untrusted channel. It never looks at the bytes of /ca.crt. index.html and cert-help.html tell the user to install the certificate if this value matches the host window. An on-path attacker who swaps the /ca.crt body and passes /ca-fingerprint through unchanged makes the page and the window match, so the user installs the attacker's root CA.
exploit_scenario: The attacker sits on the network path between a phone and the localReceiver host. When the phone opens https://<host>:<port>/, the attacker ends TLS with their own certificate. The phone does not trust the localReceiver CA yet, so it warns exactly as it would for the real server, and the user proceeds. The attacker forwards every request to the real server unchanged except GET /ca.crt, for which it returns its own root CA certificate. GET /ca-fingerprint (and the X-CA-Fingerprint-SHA256 header) pass through untouched, so cert-check.js shows the real CA fingerprint. The user compares it with the fingerprint in the host window, sees a match, and installs and fully trusts the attacker's certificate as a root CA. The page's 'If the two differ, do not install it' check passes because it compares two copies of the real fingerprint and never the certificate being installed. In --http mode (non-default) neither the page (cert-check.js:7) nor the host window (ServerWindow.java:517) shows a fingerprint, so there is no check at all.
preconditions: Attacker has an on-path position on the LAN (e.g. ARP or DHCP spoofing on the same Wi-Fi) while the victim device installs the certificate for the first time

The victim device has not yet trusted the localReceiver CA, so the browser shows the same untrusted-certificate warning for the real server and for the attacker's TLS endpoint, and the user clicks through
The victim follows the app's own install guidance (index.html footer link / cert-help.html)
recommendation: Do not treat any value rendered by the web page as the verification source. Under MITM the attacker controls the page, cert-check.js and every response, so hashing /ca.crt in the browser would not help either. Tell users to compare the host window's SHA-256 fingerprint with the one shown by the OS certificate installer or trust-store UI (iOS profile 'More Details', Android certificate details, Windows certificate dialog Details tab, macOS Keychain), which comes from the certificate bytes actually being installed. Remove or clearly caveat the page-displayed fingerprint and the X-CA-Fingerprint-SHA256 header so they are not presented as a security check. Separately, add a name-constraints extension to the CA (or stop claiming it is scoped) and do not offer CA installation in HTTP mode without an out-of-band fingerprint.

title: Pairing toggle updates the old server object after a root change, so the running server stays in open mode while the GUI shows pairing as required
impact: Pairing is silently disabled for the rest of the session while the UI reports it as enforced. Every unauthenticated LAN client gets full read and write access to the shared root, and the per-device folder scopes and deny lists are bypassed because the OPEN device is scoped to everything.
description: The pairingBox listener is a lambda inside the constructor, so `server` resolves to the constructor parameter, which shadows the field. chooseRoot() later sets the field to a new LocalReceiverServer at line 377, but every later toggle still calls setPairingRequired on the original, stopped instance. The live server's authorize() decision at Devices.java:141 keeps whatever pairing value it had when the root changed.
exploit_scenario: The operator last ran localReceiver in open mode, so pairing=false is persisted. At launch they click 'Change…' and pick a different shared folder. chooseRoot builds a new server with pairingRequired=false. The operator then ticks 'Require device pairing' and clicks Start. The tick only reaches the discarded server. startOn() mints a pairing code on the new server and the window shows a normal 'Pair:' link with a QR code, so the GUI looks fully locked down. In fact the running server returns Devices.OPEN for every request. Any host on the LAN can skip pairing and list, download, upload, rename, move and delete files across the whole shared root through /files/ and /api/*.
preconditions: The operator has 'Require device pairing' unticked (not the default; persisted via config or --open) when they use 'Change…' to pick a new file root in the same session
The operator then ticks 'Require device pairing' and starts or keeps running the server
The attacker can reach the server's port on the LAN
recommendation: Do not let constructor lambdas capture the shadowing parameter. Reference the field explicitly (this.server.setPairingRequired(...), this.server.isRunning(), this.server.devices()) in the dirBrowseBox and pairingBox listeners. Or rename the constructor parameter so the field is the only `server` in scope. Consider asserting after each toggle that server.isPairingRequired() == pairingBox.isSelected().

title: Open mode authorizes every request, including cross-site ones, with full read/write and no Origin/Host check (CSRF, and DNS rebinding over HTTP)
impact: An internet attacker, not just the trusted LAN, can delete, rename or move files in the share. In HTTP+open mode they can also exfiltrate and overwrite the entire shared folder.
description: With pairing off, authorize() returns the full-access OPEN device for any request. No handler validates Origin, Referer or Host, or uses an anti-CSRF token. Writes are plain POSTs with query-string parameters and no body, so any web page a LAN user visits can trigger them. Under --http, a DNS-rebinding page can also read every file, because the Host header is never checked.
exploit_scenario: The host runs `--open` (or turns pairing off in the GUI). A LAN user visits an attacker's page, which auto-submits `<form method=POST action="https://192.168.1.10:4646/api/files/delete?path=Photos">`. The default port 4646 and common LAN ranges make the target guessable. Over HTTPS this works once the browser trusts the app's CA, which the app tells users to install. The folder is moved to the trash, and similar forms rename/move/mkdir arbitrary guessable paths. If the server also runs `--http`, the page can DNS-rebind its own hostname to the LAN IP and, being same-origin, read `GET /api/zip` (the whole share) and use the PUT chunk endpoint to upload files. The PUT route is otherwise blocked by CORS preflight.
preconditions: Pairing disabled (`--open` / GUI toggle; non-default)
A user on the LAN visits an attacker-controlled page
For CSRF over HTTPS, the victim browser trusts the localReceiver CA; for DNS-rebinding reads, the server runs `--http`
Browser does not block public-to-private requests (e.g. Chrome Local Network Access prompt not granted)
recommendation: Reject state-changing requests whose Origin (or Referer) is not the server's own origin, and reject requests whose Host header is not a known LAN IP/hostname of the server (stops DNS rebinding). Also, or alternatively, require a custom header (e.g. X-LocalReceiver: 1) on all API calls so cross-site requests trigger a CORS preflight, and keep this protection active in open mode.

title: TLS CA private key, keystore password and device token hashes can be downloaded through /files/ and /api/zip when the shared folder contains the config directory
impact: The CA private key and the server TLS key are exposed. The CA is trusted with no name restrictions on every device that installed it, so the attacker can intercept those devices' HTTPS traffic to any site, beyond localReceiver itself. Device session-token hashes and permissions in devices.properties are also exposed.
description: The TLS secrets live in Config.dir() (default ~/.config/localreceiver: ca.p12, keystore.p12, keystore.pass, devices.properties). The shared folder defaults to user.dir, and nothing in the server stops it from containing that config directory. FilesHandler checks only that the path stays inside the device root. It hides only .localreceiver-part and .localreceiver-trash, and only in listings. So GET /files/.config/localreceiver/keystore.pass and ca.p12 reach the file read at this line. ZipHandler (lines 77-91) skips only the same two folders, so one GET /api/zip with no path packs the whole config directory.
exploit_scenario: The host starts localReceiver from their home directory and turns pairing off (or gives one device whole-folder access). A device on the LAN requests GET /files/.config/localreceiver/keystore.pass and GET /files/.config/localreceiver/ca.p12, or a single GET /api/zip. It opens ca.p12 with the password and gets the localReceiver CA private key. The user installed this CA as a trusted root on every paired phone and laptop, as the app encourages. The CA has no name constraints and is valid for 10 years, so the attacker can issue certificates for any domain and intercept those devices' HTTPS traffic to any site. The fingerprint check does not help, because the stolen CA is the genuine one. The attacker also gets keystore.p12 (the server's own key), so they can impersonate the localReceiver server. With write access they could also move away or replace devices.properties, the stored session-token hashes.
preconditions: The shared folder contains the config directory, e.g. the server is started from $HOME (the default root is the working directory), or the host passes --root ~ or a parent of it. The README tells users to put the jar in the folder they want to share; a desktop double-click launch that starts in the home directory is plausible but was not verified here.

The requester can read the whole shared folder: the server is in --open mode (pairing off, so no authentication at all), or the host widened a paired device's folder to "" (whole shared folder). A newly paired device is limited to its own subfolder by default and cannot reach the config directory.
HTTPS mode was run at least once, so ca.p12 and keystore.pass exist.
category: Files or Directories Accessible to External Parties
recommendation: Refuse to serve anything inside Config.dir(). Block paths whose real path (toRealPath) is inside the config directory in FilesHandler, ZipHandler, FileOpsHandler and UploadHandler. Refuse to start, or warn, when the file root contains the config directory. Also consider denying dot-directories by default. Keep the CA key in a non-exportable OS keystore where possible, or give the CA name constraints. Note that keytool cannot add name constraints, so this would mean generating the CA another way.

title: Unauthenticated /api/pair reveals which device names are paired (409 'taken' before the code is checked)
impact: Pre-authentication disclosure of the paired device names (and the default per-device folder names), which helps with reconnaissance and social engineering. It does not by itself grant access.
description: POST /api/pair is reachable without a session. Devices.pair() checks whether the client-supplied name is taken before it validates the pairing code. Anyone can therefore send any code with a candidate name and tell from the 409 'taken' vs 403 'code' response whether a device with that name exists. New devices' folder names are seeded from their names.
exploit_scenario: An unpaired LAN client sends `POST /api/pair?code=AAAA-AAAA&name=alice`, `...&name=dad_phone`, and so on. A 409 response confirms that the device and, by default, its folder name exist. A 403 means the name is not in use. No code is consumed and there is no rate limit.
preconditions: Network reach to the server port
Pairing mode (default)
recommendation: Validate the pairing code first, without consuming it. Only check the name for a valid code, then consume the code. This keeps the 'a rejected name does not burn the code' behaviour while hiding name existence from callers without a code.
